Climate summit warns stronger action needed to curb global warming

Reuters

07 October, 2026 06:30 am IST

Facebook

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

NADI, Fiji/SYDNEY, Oct 7 (Reuters) – Countries must urgently scale up their commitments to keep temperature rises within 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) to limit the impacts of extreme weather, a statement from a conference leading up to the UN’s COP31 summit said.

The ministerial meeting, being held in Fiji and Tuvalu, said on Tuesday that “deep, rapid and sustained emissions reductions are required to minimise the magnitude and duration of overshoot” of the target.

“As global temperature increases approach 1.5C and we face strong El Nino conditions, we reiterate that every fraction of a degree of warming accelerates the impacts of climate change and increases the risk of irreversible loss and damage for climate vulnerable communities,” the statement said.

Show Full Article

Some Pacific nations face an existential threat from rising sea levels driven by climate change. Tuvalu’s sea levels have risen about 15 cm (6 inches) in the three decades to 2023, according to NASA researchers, twice as fast as the global average.

Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, governments committed to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees above the 1850-1900 pre-industrial period, a threshold the UN’s environmental body warned last month the world would exceed “within a few years”.

The pre-COP31 conference also reaffirmed the importance of continuing sovereignty and the rights of states to maintain maritime zones under international law, even as climate-related sea-level rise threatens to reshape coastlines in the Pacific.

Pre-COP events, preparatory meetings leading up to the United Nations COP31 climate forum in Turkey in November, are typically technocratic meetings of climate negotiators.

Australia and Pacific partners are working together through the COP31 Pacific Partnership to ensure Pacific voices and solutions are at the centre of global climate action, while also seeking to strengthen regional ties ahead of the main summit.

(Reporting by Peter Hobson in Nadi and Renju Jose in Sydney; Editing by Sonali Paul)

California governor condemns Trump’s ‘let ’em take Los Angeles’ comments

Reuters

07 October, 2026 04:30 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

(Refiles to correct date in dateline, please read Oct 6 not Oct 5)

By Steve Gorman

LOS ANGELES, Oct 6 (Reuters) – California Governor Gavin Newsom has lashed out at President Donald Trump for remarks to a crowd of his supporters in Nebraska’s farm belt suggesting that Iran could “take out” a major US city like Los Angeles or San Diego.

Show Full Article

Newsom denounced the Republican president as “deranged and dangerous” following Trump’s appearance at a political rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday, about a month before midterm elections that could sweep Democrats back in control of Congress.

Trump drew fire for comments he delivered as he spoke about American wartime economic sacrifices, saying he was determined to “see a tremendous victory, because it verifies all the things we did.”

“And again, remember, with the war, it’s just artificial, it’s a little bit high, it’s a small price to pay,” he added, apparently referring to rising prices of fuel, fertilizer and other products attributed to energy market disruptions from the war.

“It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, for keeping our country safe. They could take out a city. Let ’em take out Los Angeles, let ’em take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay, and it’s going to be over with very soon,” he said.

“It’s essentially almost over with,” Trump went on. “But it’s going to end very soon, and it’s going to end one way or the other.”

Trump has shrugged off inflation concerns stemming from the Iran conflict before, and even downplayed his concerns about the potential for Iran or its allies to launch an attack on US soil.

But Monday’s comments prompted a backlash from California officials.

Newsom, a Democrat who has positioned himself as a major political foil to Trump and is considered a possible candidate for the Democratic Party’s presidential nomination in 2028, swiftly countered Trump’ Nebraska remarks on social media.

Newsom juxtaposed a video clip of Trump in Grand Island with mention of the president’s previous rhetoric to justify deploying US military troops to Los Angeles and other cities to fight crime and enforce immigration.

“After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California, Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego,” Newsom wrote on his X account.

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, a Democrat and former member of Congress, likewise chided Trump for his comments.

“The president of the United States suggested that a foreign government attack Los Angeles. His statements against our city are dangerous and could potentially compromise our safety,” Bass said in a statement.

There was no immediate response from the White House to a request by Reuters for comment on criticism of Trump’s remarks.

Los Angeles and San Diego rank as the largest and second-largest cities in California by population, and LA ranks as the second-most populous city in the nation, trailing only New York City.

(Reporting by Steve Gorman in Los Angeles; Editing by Neil Fullick)

Ukraine’s Zelenskiy says intelligence shows Russia is preparing massive attack

Reuters

06 October, 2026 11:30 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

Oct 6 (Reuters) – President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Tuesday that the latest intelligence suggested Russia was preparing a “massive attack” on Ukraine.

“There is updated intelligence indicating that Russia is preparing a massive attack,” Zelenskiy said in his nightly video address.

“Ukrainian services and our air force are ready to respond to the extent permitted by our available means of defence.”

Show Full Article

Zelenskiy said Ukraine’s position depended largely on what its allies could provide in terms of weaponry to defend against a new Russian attack.

“A great deal depends on our partners, on every leader and every country in the world that has the defensive capabilities we need and can provide them to us,” he said.

“It is critically important that there be the political will to do so, particularly in the United States, in Europe and among our other partners.”

(Reporting by Ron Popeski and Oleksandr Kozhukhar; editing by Deepa Babington)

Police fire teargas as French school protests cause ‘heaviest toll in decades’

Reuters

06 October, 2026 11:00 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

By Tilman Blasshofer, Cecile Mantovani and Lucien Libert STRASBOURG/LYON/PARIS, Oct 6 (Reuters) – Police fired tear gas at protesters outside French high schools on Tuesday as students, teachers and parents took to the streets on the biggest day of what Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu described as the most violent school protests in decades.

The protests, in which a teenager lost a hand on Monday, were the latest manifestation of public anger in a country where the far right and far left are surging ahead of a presidential election in the spring.

The government is under pressure to tame public debt amid weak growth, and has struggled with basic tasks such as passing a budget since President Emmanuel Macron’s allies lost their majority in a 2024 parliamentary vote.

Show Full Article

Lecornu told lawmakers at least 215 teenagers and 85 school staff had so far been injured in clashes, “the heaviest toll in decades paid by the school system”. His office said more than 700 police officers were also hurt.

Macron has convened Lecornu and other senior ministers at an emergency meeting on Tuesday, broadcaster BFM reported.

In Marseille and Nantes, protesters held up signs reading “The state has killed national education”. In Toulouse, parents linked arms at the front of a march through the city.

In Strasbourg, Lyon, Rennes and Paris, the demonstrations at times turned violent, with police firing tear gas and protesters lighting fires in the streets and hurling projectiles.

The Paris police said the clashes there had come about when some 300 people attempted to face off against security forces, adding that the protest was generally unfolding well elsewhere.

By late afternoon they said they were still clashing with a small contingent of people. Three storefronts had been damaged.

The protests began in September in the deprived suburbs of Paris, before spreading nationwide.

“There is such a gap between the elites and us,” said Hugo Vetzel, a recent high-school graduate in Strasbourg.

The High School Students Union said more than half of France’s high schools were blockaded or would close for the day. Some local education authorities have tried to move classes online.

Students complain about schools facing basic maintenance problems, from water leaks to rat infestations.

THOUSANDS OF ARRESTS

Rights groups, students and parent groups have accused authorities of using disproportionate force against minors. The government says the protest movement has been hijacked by outsiders and in some places deteriorated into urban violence.

France’s interior ministry said 6,100 people have been arrested since the protests began, the overwhelming majority of them minors. More than 1,800 people are being prosecuted for unspecified crimes, including 1,483 minors, the justice ministry said.

A teenager’s hand was blown off as high-school protesters clashed with riot police in northern France on Monday. The regional newspaper La Voix du Nord said the 15-year-old lost his hand and part of his lower arm after picking up a police grenade intended to be non-lethal.

“They want to divide the young people into good and bad protesters,” said Omar Slaouti, a high-school teacher in Argenteuil, a northwestern suburb of Paris. “If there were no trash cans on fire, the government would not have stepped back and become aware of the issues at stake.”

Six months before an election to replace Macron, his government and far-right leader Marine Le Pen’s National Rally party have accused hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) lawmakers and mayors of stoking the unrest. LFI denies the accusation.

“All the young people are in the streets. Everywhere there aren’t police, everything is going smoothly,” said Jean-Luc Melenchon, LFI’s presidential candidate.

PRIME MINISTER PROMISES A RESPONSE

Lecornu has ordered his ministers to tackle the students’ leading demands. Those include ensuring absent teachers are replaced, reviewing the length of the 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. school day and the need for longer lunch breaks.

The government will also look at repairs needed to ageing school buildings, said Lecornu, who demanded ministers send in their first proposals by the end of October.

Parent Emilie Lhomme said at a protest outside the Helene Boucher school in Paris that the government’s words were not enough: “That’s all fine and dandy, but that’s not what’s going to change the daily lives of our children,” she said.

Finding spare cash to implement educational reforms will be difficult.

The government is under pressure to try to narrow a ballooning budget deficit as investor concerns about France’s growing debt, weak growth and reluctance to rein in spending push the cost of borrowing higher. The yield on France’s 10-year bonds briefly hit a 24-year high of over 5% last week.

The surge in French borrowing costs has started to spill into the broader euro area, with the sliding euro currency the latest alarm bell for policy makers. Finance Minister Roland Lescure said on Tuesday there was no need for the European Central Bank to step in.

Le Pen, the far-right euro-sceptic populist leading the presidential race ahead of next spring’s election, set out plans to slash public spending if elected, seeking to establish her fiscal credibility as the bond market crisis deepens.

French spending on education has lagged inflation and the country’s students are trailing their OECD peers in overall performance, data from the PISA 2025 assessment shows.

(Reporting by Tilman Blasshofer in Strasbourg, Cecile Mantovani in Lyon, Lucien Libert, Juliette Jabkhiro, Elizabeth Pineau and Dominique Vidalon in Paris, Layli Foroudi in Argenteuil, Inti Landauro and Sudip Kar-Gupta in Brussels, and Dimitri Rhodes in Gdansk; Writing by Richard Lough and Makini Brice; Editing by Andrew Heavens and Peter Graff)
